claims.text: Adding atomic-size mismatch, mixing-entropy, and electronic-structure descriptors to a machine-learning model will significantly improve prediction of phonon thermal conductivity in single-phase metallic high-entropy alloys.
Atomic-size mismatch, mixing entropy, and electronic-structure descriptors robustly capture lattice distortions in high-entropy alloys.
The listed compositional and electronic descriptors robustly capture grain-boundary scattering mechanisms.
Lattice distortions reduce phonon thermal conductivity by enhancing phonon scattering.
Nanoscale grain-boundary features enhance phonon scattering in the alloy.
Variations in lattice distortion and electronic structure govern phonon scattering in the target alloys.
Explicit descriptor use permits more nuanced thermal-conductivity prediction than models based only on averaged compositional effects.
Training on an expanded dataset combining literature and newly measured phonon thermal conductivities will improve predictive performance.
The proposed model will improve phonon-thermal-conductivity prediction accuracy by at least 20% relative to CALPHAD or rule-of-mixtures models.
Alloys predicted to have phonon thermal conductivity below 10 W/m·K will be experimentally confirmed within ±10% of the predictions.
Current CALPHAD and conventional machine-learning approaches use averaged or less detailed compositional descriptors.
Current CALPHAD and conventional machine-learning approaches have lower prediction accuracy than the proposed model will achieve.
The approach is applicable to single-phase metallic high-entropy alloys having uniform microstructures.
The approach may not extend to multiphase or compositionally segregated systems.
Training-dataset size and quality and model overfitting are material sources of predictive uncertainty.
Dataset expansion and strict cross-validation will mitigate dataset-quality and overfitting risks.

contradictions.description: The mechanism says composition-derived descriptors capture grain-boundary scattering, but the experiment independently varies grain size while the specified model inputs do not include grain size or measured grain-boundary features. Thus the benchmark may vary a claimed mediator without providing the model a descriptor for that variation.

The initial state specifies uniform grain sizes, whereas the benchmark calls for controlled grain-size variation. This can be reconciled as uniformity within each specimen and variation between specimens, but that distinction is not stated.
